options: Microsoft.SqlServer.Management.Smo — the .NET class library for programmatically managing SQL Server, the same API SSMS itself uses
A separate third-party PowerShell module competing with dbatools
A SQL Server backup file format
A T-SQL keyword for scripting objects
questions.explain: SMO is Microsoft's .NET object model for SQL Server, and it's the same API that SQL Server Management Studio's object tree is built on.

questions.q: What object sits at the root of the SMO object model?
options: The Server object — databases, logins, jobs, and configuration all hang off it
The Database object
The Scripter object
The Login object
questions.explain: Everything in SMO branches off a Server object, which represents the whole SQL Server instance.

questions.q: What is dbatools' relationship to SMO?
options: dbatools is built partly on SMO, wrapping common SMO operations into simpler, tested cmdlets
dbatools replaced SMO entirely; SMO is deprecated
dbatools and SMO have no relationship at all
SMO is a newer module built on top of dbatools
questions.explain: dbatools' own source code calls into SMO extensively — it's a friendly, tested layer built on top of the SMO object model, not a separate technology.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, what real task did SMO's Scripter object accomplish that has no single dedicated dbatools cmdlet?
options: Generating an exact CREATE TABLE script for a table, with granular control over dependencies and scripting options
Backing up a database
Creating a new SQL login
Restarting the SQL Server service
questions.explain: SMO's Scripter object exposes many granular scripting options directly; dbatools focuses its cmdlet surface on repeatable high-level DBA tasks instead of wrapping every one.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue SMO knowledge doesn't become unnecessary just because dbatools exists?
options: dbatools covers common daily tasks well, but doesn't wrap every property or method SMO exposes, so edge cases still require dropping down to SMO directly
dbatools is being discontinued by Microsoft
SMO is actually faster than dbatools for every task
dbatools cannot connect to SQL Server at all without SMO code written by the user
questions.explain: For the roughly 80% of tasks dbatools already handles cleanly, use dbatools; for the remaining edge cases and obscure object model pieces, SMO is still the way through.
